rising.headline: Palomma Secures $10 Million Series A for Rental Financial Services
rising.teaser: Colombian startup Palomma raises Series A funding to expand landlord financing and tenant rent payment tools.
rising.whatItIs: A proptech financial platform offering payment processing and financing for landlords and property managers.
rising.whyItMatters: Modernizes cash flow management and rental collections in Latin America's expanding real estate market.
rising.bankAngle: Real estate credit and payment divisions can observe embedded financing models for property management ecosystems.
rising.imageAlt: Palomma Secures $10 Million Series A for Rental Financial Services

signalScore.rationale: Embedded rent collection and landlord working capital represent fast-growing niche credit verticals in emerging markets.

rising.longSummary:
## The story

Colombian startup Palomma has raised a $10 million Series A round led by Mexican venture firm Cometa, bringing its total funding to $14 million including a previously undisclosed $4 million, according to co-founder and chief executive Cipriano Echavarría. The round included Volpe Capital, Clocktower Technology Ventures, Tekton Ventures, Simma Capital and Yango Ventures alongside existing backers Y Combinator, 17Sigma, Nido Ventures and Norte Ventures, Crunchbase News reports.

Echavarría’s path to founding Palomma began at Morgan Stanley in New York, where a desk plaque led him to connect with Nubank founder David Vélez, also from Medellín. That connection brought Echavarría back to Colombia in late 2020 to help launch Nubank’s local operation. After nearly two years there, he teamed with MIT-trained engineers Felipe Monsalve and Nicolás Gómez del Campo — who had worked at Meta, Cobre and JPMorgan — to start Palomma. The trio entered Y Combinator in January 2023 intending to build an account-to-account payments processor for Spanish-speaking Latin America. Growth was flat for roughly a year, Echavarría said, until property managers began asking for help collecting rent.

The founders recognized structural friction on both sides of the rental transaction: tenants often paid rent early in the month but received paychecks twice monthly, while landlords depended on rental income yet struggled to borrow against it or protect against non-payment. Property managers handled collections through labor-intensive processes. Rather than acquire tenants and landlords individually, Palomma chose to reach them through property management companies as a distribution channel. The company now combines AI-driven leasing software, a payments system for rent collection and landlord payouts, and a suite of financial products for both tenants and property owners.

## Key details

Palomma reports that annual recurring revenue has grown thirtyfold in 18 months to about $3 million, according to Echavarría. The platform processes approximately $130 million in monthly rental payments, serving more than 200,000 tenants through over 500 property managers in Colombia, with an estimated $1.5 billion in annualized rent payment volume. Net revenue retention stands at 390% after 12 months, meaning revenue from existing customer cohorts nearly quadrupled even after accounting for churn and contraction, the company says.

The product stack has four main layers. Property managers pay a subscription fee for AI software that handles leasing inquiries, customer service and collections via WhatsApp. Palomma then processes rent payments, taking a percentage of volume. That payment data feeds underwriting for financial products: Palomma Plus offers tenants rewards and credit-building benefits; Palomma Advance lets landlords collect up to 12 months of future rental income upfront; Palomma Protect covers rental income if a tenant defaults; and Palomma Flex, in development, would allow tenants to split monthly rent into two installments. The company claims its leasing agent can deliver a rental-guarantee approval in under 30 seconds using data from leasing conversations and payment behavior.

Palomma initially bears the risk on rental guarantees itself but is finalizing a partnership with an insurer to share that risk and expand capacity, Echavarría told Crunchbase News. Operations are lean: as of early November the team numbered 18 employees, up from about 14 at the Series A close roughly three weeks earlier. A single customer-service employee works alongside AI agents to support the tenant base, the chief executive said.

The company plans to use the new capital to deepen its position in Colombia, develop additional AI and financial products, and prepare for expansion into other markets — Mexico, Brazil and the Spanish-speaking U.S. market are under consideration, though Colombia remains the priority. Longer term, Palomma intends to move beyond rentals into homeowners-association payments and residential property transactions.

## Why it matters

Palomma’s trajectory illustrates a pattern emerging in Latin American fintech: companies that layer financial services onto vertical software to unlock distribution and data advantages in fragmented markets. Cometa managing partner Pepe Bolaños noted that nearly 8 million households rent in Colombia alone, and that outdated processes create an opportunity to build a proprietary data asset monetizable through AI. He highlighted the founding team’s experience — Echavarría scaling Nubank’s Colombia launch, Monsalve and Gómez del Campo’s technical and financial backgrounds — and the speed of execution: roughly $130 million in monthly payment volume and 200,000 tenants served with about 14 employees at the time of investment.

The startup’s model draws comparisons to several U.S. companies — EliseAI for leasing automation, Bilt for tenant rewards, TheGuarantors for rental guarantees, Flex for rent-splitting — but Echavarría argues that Latin America’s smaller addressable markets require a broader product suite to reach comparable scale. By owning the payment rail, Palomma captures behavioral data that improves underwriting, flags potential defaults and supports new financial products, while AI keeps operational costs low. That combination of distribution through property managers, proprietary payment data and automation is the core of the competitive thesis Bolaños described.

Execution risks remain. The company’s rental-guarantee exposure is currently on its own balance sheet until the insurer partnership closes. Expansion beyond Colombia will require navigating different regulatory regimes, payment infrastructures and competitive landscapes. The heavy reliance on WhatsApp for leasing conversations ties distribution to a single platform. And the net revenue retention figure, while high, reflects a young cohort in a single geography. Still, Palomma’s early metrics suggest that the vertical-software-plus-financial-services playbook that has produced large outcomes in the United States may have a viable analogue in Latin America’s rental market.

rising.headline: Ring Confirms Home Drone Cam Operates Exclusively on Autonomous AI
rising.teaser: Ring eliminates manual steering for its indoor camera drone, relying strictly on autonomous AI navigation routes.
rising.whatItIs: An autonomous indoor home security drone that navigates pre-programmed flight paths without human pilot controls.
rising.whyItMatters: Demonstrates the rollout of fully autonomous consumer robotics despite public demonstration accidents and navigation hurdles.
rising.imageAlt: Ring Confirms Home Drone Cam Operates Exclusively on Autonomous AI

signalScore.rationale: Illustrates consumer hardware manufacturers removing human manual overrides in favor of fully autonomous systems.

rising.longSummary:
## The story
The Ring Drone Cam is a home security device that will operate without any user‑controlled pilot when it becomes available in January. The product relies entirely on an “AI Pilot” system that follows pre‑programmed routes and navigates around obstacles without human input. Ring announced that customers will not be able to manually steer the drone, a change from an early development stage in which manual controls were demonstrated. In a video broadcast on CBS Mornings and later posted on Threads, Ring founder Jamie Siminoff allowed reporter Jo Ling Kent to operate an early prototype using a mobile app. The footage captured two crashes: the first was attributed by Ring to a malfunction in collision‑avoidance technology, and the second showed the drone striking a wall after failing to respond to manual inputs. Siminoff explained that the second crash occurred because the drone lost internet connectivity, a condition that also disables autonomous flight. He added that the system is designed to stop and land if connectivity is lost, but the demonstration showed that this safeguard did not activate. “If it loses connectivity, it’s supposed to stop and land.” “Yeah, so we can load manual controls.”

## Key details
The Ring Drone Cam’s AI Pilot system is responsible for all flight decisions, including takeoff, route following, and obstacle avoidance. The device is programmed to fly along predetermined paths that have been set by the user or the device itself, and it is expected to navigate indoor spaces without requiring a human operator. Ring has indicated that the drone will rely on continuous internet connectivity to receive updates and to maintain its autonomous functions; loss of connectivity is supposed to trigger an automatic landing. During development, Ring experimented with manual flight controls that allowed a user to pilot the drone via a mobile app. In the CBS News demonstration, Siminoff confirmed that manual controls were available at that stage, saying, “Yeah, so we can load manual controls.” However, the company later stated that manual piloting will not be offered when the product launches in January. Ring spokesperson Sam McGee said the company explored many features but concluded that autonomous flight to patrol points provides the best customer benefit and experience. The company declined to provide a demonstration of the app to The Verge and said the device will operate only on pre‑programmed routes. The video of the CBS demo, which showed two crashes, highlighted technical challenges such as collision‑avoidance failures and connectivity loss, and raised questions about the reliability of fully autonomous home robots.

## Why it matters
The Ring Drone Cam illustrates the growing push toward fully autonomous consumer robotics, a trend that could reshape how home security devices are designed and used. By removing manual piloting, Ring signals confidence that its AI system can reliably navigate indoor environments without direct user oversight. The demonstration accidents raise questions about the robustness of autonomous navigation and the adequacy of safety mechanisms, especially regarding connectivity loss and obstacle detection. If the product launches without the ability to intervene manually, consumers may face higher expectations for reliability, and any failure could erode trust in similar devices from other manufacturers. The incident also invites scrutiny from regulators and safety advocates who may examine how companies test and certify autonomous home robots. Moreover, the lack of manual controls could limit the device’s appeal to users who prefer direct control or who are uncomfortable with fully autonomous technology. As the market for smart home robotics expands, the Ring Drone Cam’s approach may influence standards for autonomous operation, user consent, and data privacy, given that the drone relies on internet connectivity to function. Ultimately, the product’s success will depend on whether the AI Pilot can consistently avoid collisions and handle edge cases without human assistance, setting a benchmark for future autonomous consumer devices.

rising.headline: Flight Attendants Union Halts Employee Records From Google Data Sale
rising.teaser: Flight attendants union strikes a deal with Google to exclude sensitive worker records from data transaction.
rising.whatItIs: An agreement removing employee data from a $10 million data asset sale involving defunct airline assets.
rising.whyItMatters: Establishes labor union precedent for intervening in corporate bankruptcy and distressed asset data transactions.
rising.bankAngle: Restructuring and workout teams must navigate employee privacy covenants during distressed asset liquidations.
rising.imageAlt: Flight Attendants Union Halts Employee Records From Google Data Sale

signalScore.rationale: Distressed asset data sales increasingly face legal intervention regarding employee personal data rights.

rising.longSummary:
## The story
The flight attendants union representing Spirit Airlines employees says it has reached an agreement that removes employee records from a data sale involving the defunct airline’s assets. The deal is part of the liquidation process after Spirit Airlines ceased operations earlier this year. In August, representatives for the budget airline said in a legal brief that it would sell decades of data to Google for about $10 million. Google said it would not receive personal information as part of the sale, according to the article. The union, the 55,000-member Association for Flight Attendants, argued that Google’s proposed safeguards would not prevent serious privacy violations for Spirit flight attendants.

The article notes that privacy concerns often focus on personal chatbots and consumer data, but employees mostly do not have a choice about whether their information is used. A new, multibillion-dollar industry is dedicated to selling and buying work files and emails for AI training, and it is growing. Data privacy laws tend to focus on consumer protections and rarely consider the rights of workers who create that information.

The dispute centered on a large set of employee information, including 1.99 billion emails, 664 million Microsoft Teams messages, and employee travel and training information dating back to 1986, the article said. The union raised concerns about sensitive records, including medical records, documents related to investigations and labor relations, and information about industry-wide safety management systems.

Under the revised deal, Spirit would hire a third-party data de-identification company called Tonic AI to exclude information that could be associated with individual employees or consumers and to ensure data could not be relinked to specific people. Google has promised to keep the data in de-identified form, according to the article. The agreement also includes an opt-out clause, allowing Google to back out if the data-cleaning process reduces the assets by more than 8 percent. Google did not respond to a request for comment.

A judge still needs to approve the agreement next week.

## Key details
The proposed settlement is described as first-of-its-kind and is part of the liquidation of Spirit Airlines. The revised deal requires Tonic AI to exclude potentially identifying information and to prevent relinking. Google has promised to maintain the de-identified data. Many sensitive records will be excluded from the sale, including medical records, documents related to employee investigations and labor relations, and information about industry-wide safety management systems.

In early November, a trade organization representing airlines said including that information could make employees less willing to come forward to report safety issues through voluntary programs, which are widely regarded as critical to the US aviation industry’s safety record.

The agreement also includes an opt-out clause. Google can choose to renounce the sale if the data-cleaning process reduces the assets by more than 8 percent.

Association for Flight Attendants President Sara Nelson told WIRED she was surprised flight attendants are at the forefront of AI-related workers’ rights issues, which often focus on employees who willingly or unwillingly train AI models. She said it is very hard to replace a flight attendant and that the issue is relevant even in jobs thought to be most protected from AI. Nelson said the union will immediately begin to demand that other airlines include worker-data-protection clauses in their labor agreements and has begun meeting with state-level politicians about legislation.

Professor Ari Ezra Waldman, a professor at the UC Irvine School of Law, called the proposed settlement a good outcome for Spirit employees. He said the deal may mean unions will know to negotiate to protect privacy rights in future data asset sales. He also pointed to banning the sale of data altogether as another possible alternative.

## Why it matters
The agreement could establish a labor precedent for handling employee data in bankruptcy and distressed asset sales. It suggests unions may need to intervene when companies sell or license worker information, especially as AI companies seek training data.

The case matters because worker information can include emails, messages, medical details, and safety-related documents. A multibillion-dollar industry is emerging that buys such data for AI training, while privacy protections for workers remain less developed than consumer protections.

The outcome is not final because a judge must approve it. Even so, the proposed deal is being described as first-of-its-kind. If approved, it could shape how unions and companies handle worker data in future AI-related transactions.

The story matters beyond Spirit Airlines because similar data sales could occur at other companies. Nelson said the union will begin demanding worker-data-protection clauses at other airlines, and the group has started meeting with state-level politicians about writing worker data protections into law.

The broader debate continues. Tech leaders have argued that workers understand their information will train AI models and that AI can bring benefits. Nelson said US workers are not buying the upside of AI and that the vision of AI abundance is out of step with growing wariness of technology.

africa.headline: South African Fintechs Expand Beyond Payments Into Direct Merchant Financing
africa.teaser: Companies like Yoco, Optasia, and Paymenow utilize transaction history to deliver merchant financing and consumer credit.
africa.whatItIs: Merchant financing initiatives by payments providers using proprietary transaction records to extend credit.
africa.whyItMatters: Demonstrates the global trend of payment processors capturing SME lending revenue through embedded transaction data.
africa.bankAngle: Highlights how non-bank payment rails use merchant transaction flows to disintermediate traditional business overdrafts and loans.
africa.imageAlt: South African Fintechs Expand Beyond Payments Into Direct Merchant Financing

signalScore.rationale: Payment-linked underwriting allows African fintechs to capture lucrative small-business lending margins.

africa.longSummary:
## The story

South Africa’s fintechs have spent years making it easier to move money. Now they want to help people and businesses access it when they need it most. Yoco’s $100 million credit facility from Victory Park Capital, a United States investment firm, is the latest sign of that shift. The South African payments and fintech company is expanding its cash advances business, betting that transaction data can help it finance small businesses that traditional banks struggle to assess.

The article says the opportunity is substantial, but financing requires more than customer numbers and transaction volumes. It demands capital, risk management and the ability to finance responsibly to customers whose financial circumstances can change quickly. The next phase of South Africa’s fintech boom will depend on whether companies can turn transaction data and customer relationships into sustainable financing businesses.

For Yoco, financing extends its relationship with independent businesses through card machines, point-of-sale software and online payments. The company has advanced more than R6.5 billion ($395 million) to over 40,000 merchants since 2018, working with specialist credit providers. Its new facility is expected to give it greater control over the pricing and risk of its cash advances operation. Yoco uses sales data to assess merchants and present funding offers through its app. Advances range from R2,000 ($122) to R1.5 million, with repayments deducted from daily takings rather than fixed monthly instalments.

## Key details

Yoco is not alone. South Africa’s fintech giants, Yoco, Optasia and Paymenow, are pursuing this opportunity from different angles, responding to a common problem: consumers and small businesses need more than payment services to manage their finances.

Optasia built its business around airtime advances distributed through telecommunications operators, and is shifting towards broader microfinance services for consumers and small businesses. The company generated $270 million in revenue during the first nine months of 2026, up 45% year-on-year. Microfinance contributed $194 million, or approximately 72% of group revenue, as Optasia pursued its ambition to derive more than 80% of revenue from these services.

Optasia says its technology analyses behavioural patterns and transaction signals to assess customers with limited formal credit histories. But the article adds that identifying a potential borrower does not automatically mean financing is affordable or appropriate. Optasia says its technology assesses not only whether customers qualify but also how much they can borrow and realistically afford to repay.

Paymenow, an employee financial wellness and earned-wage access fintech, approaches the problem differently. It allows employees to access wages they have already earned before payday. By 2026, the company reported serving more than 750,000 employees across South Africa, Namibia, Zambia and Pakistan. Its merger with PayCurve in May broadened its offering beyond wage access to include debt rehabilitation, savings and financial education.

## Why it matters

The article frames this as part of a broader global trend: payment processors capturing SME lending revenue through embedded transaction data. The opportunity is substantial. The 2025 Finfind and African Bank SA MSME Access to Finance Report estimates South Africa’s small-business financing gap at R350 billion ($21.3 billion). Small and medium-sized enterprises receive just 13% of national bank lending, compared with 51% for large corporations.

For fintechs, the gap offers an opportunity to build new revenue streams around customers they already serve. But the economics are more complicated than identifying demand. Fintechs already have customer relationships, transaction data and digital distribution networks. Financing can deepen those relationships while creating revenue beyond payments. Yet capital has a cost, defaults erode returns, and data cannot eliminate uncertainty when household budgets and small-business revenues remain under pressure.

Yoco says it has not recorded an unprofitable cohort of cash advances since beginning operations in 2018, including during the Covid-19 pandemic. However, it has not disclosed cohort-level performance figures, default rates or write-offs alongside its latest facility announcement. Those details will become important as the business scales.

The risks around access are also clear. FinMark Trust found that 75% of South Africans who borrowed in 2024 used credit to cover essentials such as food. Nedbank’s 2024 Financial Health Monitor found that 10% of workers had turned to payday lenders to manage financial stress, while 12% had borrowed from informal lenders. The figures highlight demand for short-term financial support, but also the risk that financing could deepen the pressures it is meant to ease.

For merchant cash advances, flexible repayments can help businesses manage fluctuating sales, but deductions from daily takings may leave less money for stock, wages and operating costs when revenue falls. The same logic applies to earned-wage access, where accessing earned wages may offer an alternative to expensive short-term borrowing, but long-term value depends on whether it improves financial management rather than simply shifting pressure to an earlier point in the month.

South Africa’s fintechs have made financial services more accessible. Their next test is whether they can turn that access into sustainable businesses. For a merchant waiting to restock or a worker counting down to payday, success is not another transaction. It is having enough money to keep going.

africa.headline: Vodacom Deepens Mobile Financial Services Across Africa Through Safaricom Stake
africa.teaser: Vodacom targets growth beyond South Africa, leveraging its Safaricom stake to lead digital financial services.
africa.whatItIs: Strategic expansion by a telecommunications giant focusing on continental mobile money and digital banking.
africa.whyItMatters: Telecom-led mobile money platforms remain the dominant digital finance infrastructure across sub-Saharan Africa.
africa.bankAngle: Partnering with or competing against telecom-led wallets is essential for banks entering African retail markets.
africa.imageAlt: Vodacom Deepens Mobile Financial Services Across Africa Through Safaricom Stake

signalScore.rationale: Telco dominance in continental mobile money poses ongoing structural competition to traditional retail banking networks.

africa.longSummary:
## Story
Vodacom, a pan-African technology group, is expanding its mobile financial services across the continent through its acquisition of a controlling stake in Safaricom, East Africa's largest telecommunications company. The deal positions Vodacom to diversify beyond traditional mobile connectivity and accelerate its financial services business. With 250 million customers across Africa, Vodacom reports revenue of R102.5 billion ($6.2 billion) for the six months ended 30 September 2026, a 25.6% year-on-year increase driven partly by Safaricom's consolidation. The acquisition, completed with Vodacom increasing its shareholding to 55%, makes Safaricom a subsidiary from June 30, giving Vodacom greater exposure to Kenya's mobile money ecosystem and one of the continent's most established fintech platforms. The company's international business achieved normalised service revenue growth of 13.7%, while Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) increased 15.9%. This strategic move is part of Vodacom's broader ambition to evolve beyond calls, data, and connectivity into a broader FinTech platform.

## Key details
The article provides several specific figures and developments. Vodacom added 26 million customers over the past 12 months, bringing its total customer base to 250 million across Africa. Safaricom served 108 million financial services customers, who accessed and initiated more than $575.5 billion in transaction value over the last 12 months. Financial services revenue grew 99% to R15.9 billion ($966 million) in the reported half-year, though this figure reflects Safaricom's consolidation for only one quarter. On a pro-forma basis, including Safaricom in the comparative period, growth was 19.2%. The company's international business achieved normalised service revenue growth of 13.7%, with Vodacom's EBITDA margin reaching 37.4% in South Africa, its highest level in several years. In South Africa, Vodacom returned its prepaid business to growth, supported by higher data consumption, while cost optimisation lifted its EBITDA margin to 37.4%. The Safaricom acquisition is central to Vodacom's ambition to diversify beyond traditional mobile connectivity and accelerate its financial services business. Vodacom and Safaricom both generated pro-forma financial services revenue of R43.1 billion ($2.6 billion) over the last 12 months. The combined platforms served 108 million financial services customers. Following the acquisition, Vodacom raised its 2030 target for these businesses from 30% to more than 32%. The group declared an interim dividend of 355 cents per share, up 7.6%, supported by headline earnings per share growth of 25.7% to 587 cents. The company invested R13.3 billion ($806 million) in capital expenditure during the half, up 41%, expanding network capacity and adding infrastructure to support rising data consumption and digital services.

## Why it matters
This expansion represents a strategic shift for Vodacom from a traditional telecommunications company to a diversified fintech platform. The integration of Safaricom's mobile money ecosystem, particularly M-Pesa, provides Vodacom with a large base of financial services customers and a platform for expanding into savings, investments, credit, and other digital financial products. The article notes that financial services, fixed connectivity, digital and Internet of Things (IoT) services now account for 27.4% of Vodacom's service revenue, indicating a significant shift in business mix. The growth in financial services revenue (99% to R15.9 billion) demonstrates the commercial viability of the combined platform. For the broader African market, this consolidation strengthens Vodacom's position as it pursues Vision 2030 ambitions, with the group raising its 2030 target for these businesses from 30% to more than 32%. The international markets, particularly Egypt, Kenya, Tanzania, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), and Lesotho, are outpacing the more mature South African domestic business, suggesting that Vodacom's growth strategy is geographically diversified. The company's ability to serve 250 million customers across Africa and the $575.5 billion in transaction value processed by its financial services platforms highlight the scale of the opportunity. The strategic rationale is clear: by combining Vodacom's connectivity infrastructure with Safaricom's established mobile money platform, Vodacom aims to create one of the continent's largest FinTech platforms that can expand access to formal financial services and enable greater economic participation for millions of people and businesses. The investment of R13.3 billion in capital expenditure to support this expansion underscores the seriousness of the commitment.

africa.whatItIs: Market recovery in Nigerian telecom subscriber base following regulatory national identity number verifications.
africa.whyItMatters: Restores and clarifies the addressable digital identity and mobile payment user base in Africa's largest economy.
africa.bankAngle: Provides a validated customer baseline for mobile banking and identity verification across Nigerian financial services.
africa.imageAlt: Nigeria Active Mobile Subscriptions Reach 200 Million Following Identification Purge

signalScore.rationale: Clean digital identity data in mobile telecoms improves customer onboarding and KYC reliability for fintechs.

africa.longSummary:
## The story

Nigeria’s active mobile subscriptions reached about 200 million in September 2026, according to data from the Nigerian Communications Commission reported by TechCabal. The figure represents a recovery after a sharp decline caused by the enforcement of the National Identification Number, or NIN, linkage policy for SIM cards. The regulator’s data show active subscriptions rose 29% over two years to 200.3 million, but the market remains highly concentrated, with MTN and Airtel together accounting for about 86% of active connections.

The milestone is important because it follows a period in which reported connections fell sharply as operators disconnected SIM cards that could not be linked to verified national identity records. The article notes that the 200 million figure refers to active phone lines, not unique individuals. One person may hold multiple SIMs, and active connections can include devices such as routers. The recovery therefore signals a larger base of connected lines, but it does not by itself prove that 200 million people are using mobile phones.

## Key details

The NCC’s latest figures show MTN with 104.6 million active subscriptions in September 2026, while Airtel had 68 million. Globacom had 23.5 million, and T2 had 3.6 million. TechCabal says MTN and Airtel collectively accounted for about 172.7 million of the roughly 200.1 million connections recorded across the four operators. This concentration means that any bank or fintech relying on mobile channels will still depend heavily on the commercial terms, network quality, and regulatory relationships of the two largest operators.

The NIN-SIM policy was introduced in 2020, but enforcement intensified in 2024 as operators completed verification and disconnected lines without valid NIN records. The NCC set September 14, 2024, as the final deadline for the exercise. In its 2024 year-end performance report, the commission said active subscriptions fell from 224.7 million in 2023 to 164.9 million in 2024, a loss of 59.8 million connections, or 26.6%. The NCC attributed the decline to the removal of SIM cards not linked to verifiable NINs and to correcting a major discrepancy in one operator’s subscriber figures. By August 2024, the regulator said more than 153 million SIM cards had been linked to NINs, representing 96% compliance.

The rebound has been accompanied by higher data usage. TechCabal reports that data consumption grew about 51% year-on-year in September 2026 to 1.73 million terabytes. Network technology remains mixed: 4G accounted for 54.37% of mobile connections, 5G for 5.05%, 2G for 36.42%, and 3G for 4.16%. The continued presence of 2G and 3G suggests that many users still rely on slower networks, which can affect the design of mobile-first financial services, especially those that use USSD, SMS, or low-bandwidth apps.

Fixed broadband is also expanding. The NCC’s figures show fibre-to-the-X subscriptions, covering connections to homes, offices, streets, and hubs, increased by about 67% between the first and third quarters of 2026. The article says this points to growth in fibre access beyond mobile networks. In addition, telecommunications contributed 9.72% to Nigeria’s GDP in the second quarter of 2026, up from 9.20% in the same period of 2025. The NCC noted that figures for late 2024 and early 2025 were affected by the National Bureau of Statistics’ GDP rebasing, so comparisons across periods should be treated carefully.

## Why it matters

For a bank product team, the main significance is that Nigeria’s addressable digital identity and mobile connectivity base is becoming clearer after a disruptive regulatory cleanup. The NIN-SIM exercise may improve the reliability of customer identification data, which is relevant for know-your-customer checks, onboarding, fraud controls, and mobile payment services. At the same time, the episode shows that identity verification can reduce reported connections quickly, so banks and fintechs should not assume that subscriber growth is smooth or that every active SIM represents a usable, verified customer.

The dominance of MTN and Airtel matters for distribution. Mobile money, USSD banking, airtime top-ups, data bundles, and app-based services often depend on operator agreements and network reach. If two companies control most active connections, product strategies may need to account for pricing, interoperability, and service quality differences across networks. The smaller shares held by Globacom and T2 may still be relevant for niche segments, but they are less likely to support nationwide scale on their own.

The data also point to a gradual shift toward richer digital services. Higher data consumption and growth in 4G and fibre suggest that Nigerians are using more bandwidth-intensive applications, which can support mobile banking, video-based customer service, and digital merchant tools. However, the large share of 2G and 3G connections means that low-bandwidth and offline-capable features remain important. For a bank, this argues for product designs that work across devices and network conditions rather than assuming universal smartphone or high-speed internet access.

Finally, the telecom sector’s contribution to GDP shows that connectivity is now a core part of Nigeria’s economic infrastructure. Changes in regulation, identity policy, or network investment can therefore affect not only telecom operators but also banks, merchants, government services, and consumers. The NIN-SIM recovery is a reminder that digital growth in large emerging markets can be shaped as much by policy and identity systems as by consumer demand.

## Story
TechCabal reports that Ghana’s communications ministry has set a target of 70 percent 5G coverage across the country by March 2027. Samuel Nartey George, Ghana’s minister of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, announced the goal at an International Telecommunication Union conference in Qatar. The target represents a significant shift for a nation that recently restructured its 5G rollout approach. Initially, the government entrusted 5G infrastructure development to Next Gen InfraCo, a shared telecoms company granted exclusive rights to build a wholesale network for ten years. Mobile operators were expected to rent capacity rather than build their own. By mid-2026, the model had stalled: reports indicated that Next Gen InfraCo had activated only about 49 sites, and major operators had not signed on to use its network. In response, Ghana’s National Communications Authority ended the company’s exclusivity in July 2026, opening 5G spectrum licensing to competing operators. By October of that year, MTN Ghana and Telecel had received 5G permits. The government is also completing 2,016 rural telecommunications sites and upgrading existing networks to support faster connectivity. The move signals a policy pivot toward competition as a means to accelerate deployment. Ghana’s leadership has framed the reform as necessary to meet growing data demand and to position the country within regional digital integration efforts.

## Key details
The 70 percent coverage target by March 2027 is ambitious given Ghana’s recent experience with its original rollout plan. Under the previous arrangement, Next Gen InfraCo held exclusive rights for a decade, with operators paying to access a single wholesale network. However, by May 2026, the company had reportedly established just 49 tower sites, and no major mobile operators had committed to rent its capacity. The National Communications Authority’s decision in July 2026 to lift exclusivity opened the door for multiple operators to obtain individual 5G licences. MTN Ghana and Telecel were among the first to receive permits by October 2026. Beyond spectrum licensing, the ministry is overseeing the completion of 2,016 rural telecom sites and upgrading legacy networks to be compatible with 5G frequencies. These infrastructure upgrades aim to extend coverage beyond urban centers. The transition from a single-infra model to a competitive licensing regime marks the most visible change in Ghana’s telecom policy in recent years. Whether the new framework will translate into faster deployment remains to be seen, but the structural shift is already underway. Stakeholders will be monitoring whether the new licensing framework reduces deployment timelines and improves rural reach in the coming months.

## Why it matters
Faster, more widespread 5G coverage could directly impact real-time mobile banking and low-latency digital transactions across Ghana’s economy. The ministry’s goal of 70 percent coverage by early 2027 aligns with broader efforts to deepen financial inclusion through mobile platforms. However, infrastructure alone does not guarantee usage. The ministry acknowledges that affordable smartphones and data prices are key to actual usage. Affordable smartphones, data pricing, and consumer demand remain decisive factors. The policy shift from an exclusive wholesale model to competing operators may lower entry barriers, but historical patterns suggest that tower density does not automatically translate into active users. Ghana’s experience will be closely watched by other markets considering similar infra reforms. For the banking sector, expanded 5G could enable faster payment processing, richer digital services, and broader reach in underserved regions—provided that end-user costs and device availability keep pace with network rollout. The success of this target will depend as much on the ecosystem around the network as on the network itself. If those conditions align, the benefits for digital finance and broader economic activity could be substantial.

## The story

Ghana’s Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Samuel Nartey George, has urged Commonwealth member states to strengthen cooperation and coordinate their positions to advance shared interests at the ongoing International Telecommunication Union (ITU) Plenipotentiary Conference 2026 (PP-26) in Doha, Qatar.

Speaking as Chair of the Commonwealth ITU Group at a high-level roundtable of Commonwealth member states, the Minister called for collective action to influence global telecommunications and digital policies, particularly on issues affecting developing countries and underserved populations. The diplomatic initiative advocates coordinated regulatory stances on emerging technologies and connectivity among Commonwealth nations. It promotes equitable representation and unified digital infrastructure frameworks across emerging market economies.

Mr. George noted that approximately two billion people remain unconnected globally, and he stressed that the Commonwealth must leverage its collective influence to advance universal connectivity, digital inclusion and equitable access to emerging technologies.

He acknowledged that member states have varying priorities, but said their shared interests provide a strong foundation for cooperation. He highlighted spectrum access and satellite connectivity as key priorities for small island states, investment and last-mile connectivity for developing countries, and innovation and security for more advanced economies.

The Minister urged delegates to identify common ground, agree on issues requiring coordinated positions during committee and plenary deliberations, and establish a clear plan of action to strengthen the group’s influence throughout the conference.

The roundtable also offered candidates from Commonwealth member states seeking positions within the ITU an opportunity to present their cases and solicit support from fellow members. Ghana, which currently chairs the Commonwealth ITU Group, is seeking re-election to the ITU Council for Region D and the Radio Regulations Board.

Mr. George said Ghana would present its case alongside other candidates, emphasizing the need to provide all contestants with a fair opportunity to engage member states and seek their support.

Reaffirming the importance of Commonwealth solidarity, he called on members to harmonise their positions, strengthen mutual support and work towards an inclusive, secure and resilient digital future. He added that the Commonwealth’s strength lies in its ability to unite countries of different sizes and levels of development to achieve outcomes that individual nations might struggle to secure independently.

## Key details

The central actor in the story is Samuel Nartey George, Ghana’s Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations. He is also Chair of the Commonwealth ITU Group. His remarks were made at a high-level roundtable of Commonwealth member states during the ITU PP-26 in Doha, Qatar.

The Minister’s call is for Commonwealth states to cooperate and coordinate positions. The note says Mr. George recognised different national priorities. For small island states, the key priorities include spectrum access and satellite connectivity. The Minister asked delegates to find common ground and agree on issues for coordinated positions during committee and plenary deliberations. There is also a procedural dimension. Ghana currently chairs the Commonwealth ITU Group and is seeking re-election to the ITU Council for Region D and the Radio Regulations Board. Ghana said it would present its case with other candidates and stressed the need for fair opportunity for all contestants.

## Why it matters

The briefing concerns global digital policy coordination. If Commonwealth states harmonise their positions, it could affect how the bloc addresses telecommunications, spectrum, satellite connectivity, investment, last-mile access, innovation and security. The article frames this as a way to address the connectivity gap and to give developing and underserved populations a stronger voice in global digital rules.

The Minister’s argument is that small island states, developing countries and advanced economies have different priorities, but shared interests can support cooperation. That may matter for policy design because global standards and allocations often have consequences beyond one country.

The call for a clear plan of action and coordinated positions during committee and plenary deliberations suggests the Commonwealth group may seek more formal influence at the ITU. For stakeholders outside the immediate policy debate, the practical question is how such coordination affects digital infrastructure, telecommunications policy and technology access.

For a bank or financial institution, related areas can include digital payments, regulatory expectations, data protection, cybersecurity and inclusive access to financial services, though the article itself does not go into those details. The briefing should therefore be read as a diplomatic and policy signal rather than a market or investment recommendation.

The story is also personal and procedural: Ghana’s leadership of the Commonwealth ITU Group is being used as a platform to build consensus and advance collective interests. The Minister’s public remarks are part of a larger effort to strengthen the group’s influence at the ITU conference. The outcome could depend on whether member states agree on common positions and how they support candidates such as Ghana’s for regional and board roles.
